periods.analysis: At 3.6%, the teacher vacancy rate is in yellow, above our <=2.0% goal but below the 4.0% red line; because this is the first reported quarter, there is no quarter-over-quarter movement to report. I read this as a manageable staffing gap, not a system failure, but every unfilled classroom in Harborview has a face, a schedule, and a student attached to it. The pressure is concentrated in special education, secondary math, and airport-corridor schools where late-summer housing costs made accepted offers harder to convert into signed contracts. HR’s August hiring room at the Seaport Professional Center cleared several elementary openings, but the watch item is the substitute-covered sections at Bayfront Middle and East Harbor High.
periods.recommendations: Keep the weekly vacancy huddle in place through October, with HR, principals, and finance reviewing every open requisition by school and certification area. Extend the early-signing stipend to hard-to-staff special education and math roles, but require principals to pair it with a 30-day onboarding plan. Launch a Harborview housing-cost follow-up call for declined offers so we can distinguish compensation issues from relocation and commute barriers.

periods.analysis: The rate improved to 2.9%, down 0.7 percentage points from 3.6%, which is real progress while still leaving us in yellow rather than at the <=2.0% target. The October credential-clearing clinic with Coastal State University and the expedited background-check lane helped move candidates into classrooms before the winter break. We also saw better retention among first-year teachers assigned mentors through the Harborview New Educator Cohort, especially on the Route 12 school corridor. The watch item is that vacancies are now less numerous but more specialized, particularly speech-language pathology and upper-level science.
periods.recommendations: Sustain the credential clinic model and schedule the next one before spring student-teacher placements are finalized. Build a small, centrally managed pool of certified long-term substitutes for science, special education, and speech services rather than leaving each principal to compete alone. Ask HR to produce a declined-offer dashboard by December close so compensation, housing, and timing barriers are visible.

periods.analysis: Teacher vacancy edged down to 2.8%, a 0.1 percentage-point improvement from 2.9%, keeping us in yellow and close to where we ended the calendar year. The smaller movement tells me the broad vacancies have largely been worked down, but the remaining openings are harder to solve with standard posting and referral tools. Midyear retirements at Harborview High and a maternity-leave cluster in the North Inlet feeder pattern kept the rate from moving more decisively toward green. The watch item is whether spring recruitment starts early enough to prevent these same schools from entering summer understaffed.
periods.recommendations: Open 2025-26 hiring authorization for high-need campuses before budget adoption, using conditional offers tied to board-approved allocations. Sustain mentor stipends for the Harborview New Educator Cohort, because retention is now as important as recruitment. Direct talent staff to visit Coastal State, Tidewater Teachers College, and the bilingual certification program at St. Anselm before April 15 with school-specific openings in hand.

periods.analysis: The vacancy rate rose to 3.3%, up 0.5 percentage points from 2.8%, so the measure remains yellow but is moving the wrong way. This is the spring churn we expected, but the size of the increase deserves attention: resignations tied to regional housing costs and retirements filed after contract renewal were heavier than projected. The highest exposure is in K-5 dual language, middle-school math, and special education resource rooms serving students with interrupted attendance patterns. The watch item is conversion speed from candidate interview to signed offer, where several principals reported losing finalists to neighboring districts within 72 hours.
periods.recommendations: Set a 48-hour offer standard for hard-to-staff roles and give HR authority to issue contingent offers after principal panel approval. Extend the Harborview Teacher Residency interviews into June and reserve slots for dual-language and special education candidates. Convene finance and city housing partners to package relocation information for incoming teachers, including verified units near the Blue Line and Route 7 bus corridors.

periods.analysis: Vacancy ticked up again to 3.4%, an increase of 0.1 percentage points from 3.3%, which keeps us in yellow and too close to the 4.0% red threshold for comfort. The increase is modest, but August staffing is when modest gaps become daily operational strain for principals and families. The rapid-response hiring lab filled several elementary posts, yet secondary math, special education, and bilingual openings at South Dock, Mariner, and East Harbor remained stubborn. The watch item is burnout among returning teachers who are covering split rosters during the first six weeks of school.
periods.recommendations: Deploy a central coverage team for the first grading period so schools with vacancies are not relying only on internal class splits. Sustain the rapid-response hiring lab, but add same-day transcript review and certification pre-screening with the state licensing liaison on site. Require each school above the district average vacancy rate to submit a two-page coverage and retention plan by the second Friday in September.

periods.analysis: The rate improved to 2.8%, down 0.6 percentage points from 3.4%, returning us to the best level seen in this series while still yellow against the <=2.0% goal. That improvement reflects disciplined execution: the central coverage team stabilized September, and the fall hiring lab converted late candidates into signed contracts before Thanksgiving. Mentor logs from the New Educator Cohort show fewer emergency support requests in the airport-corridor schools, which suggests the work is taking hold beyond the spreadsheet. The watch item is keeping this gain through winter, when specialized vacancies can reopen quickly after leaves and retirements.
periods.recommendations: Sustain the central coverage team through January, but narrow its deployment to special education, bilingual, and secondary math vacancies so we do not dilute impact. Extend stay interviews to all first- and second-year teachers at schools that improved since 2025-Q3, and code the themes by workload, leadership support, and commute cost. Prepare a winter vacancy risk list using known leave requests, retirement notices, and expiring provisional certifications.

periods.analysis: Teacher vacancy held at 2.8%, with 0.0 percentage-point movement from 2.8%, so we are stable but still in yellow. Stability after winter break is a positive sign in a fast-growing city where enrollment, housing costs, and labor competition all move at once. The risk is that a flat result can breed comfort; we are still 0.8 percentage points above the <=2.0% target, and the same certification areas continue to carry the burden. The watch item is the spring pipeline, particularly whether resident teachers and student teachers are being matched now to the campuses most likely to have openings.
periods.recommendations: Lock in early contracts for high-performing residents before spring break, starting with South Dock, Bayfront Middle, and East Harbor High. Sustain the stay-interview process and convert the findings into principal coaching actions, not just HR notes. Build a named candidate pipeline by subject area, with weekly status on offers, certification, background checks, and relocation needs.

periods.analysis: The rate increased to 3.2%, up 0.4 percentage points from 2.8%, keeping us in yellow and signaling that spring separations again outpaced our early hiring gains. This is not a crisis, but it is a warning light: Harborview’s growth is creating more classrooms, and the regional labor market is not handing us certified teachers on demand. HR reports that several accepted candidates delayed start dates because of housing searches, while special education and middle-school math remain the tightest pools. The watch item for summer is speed and precision, because entering August near 3.2% leaves little margin before schools feel the strain.
periods.recommendations: Move to a summer staffing command center with twice-weekly vacancy reviews by school, route cluster, and certification area until the rate is back below 3.0%. Sustain early contracts where they worked, but add a relocation concierge for accepted candidates who need housing, licensing, and onboarding help within a two-week window. Prioritize special education and middle-school math with targeted signing incentives, principal-level interview blocks, and named backup candidates for every remaining opening.

periods.analysis: The teacher vacancy rate fell from 3.2% to 2.9%, an improvement after spring separations. It remains above the 2% target, with shortage-area hiring still requiring close attention.
periods.recommendations: Continue campus-by-campus vacancy reviews and prioritize special education and middle-school math placements and onboarding.
